rv.q: Just as jazz musicians take a well-known melody and give it a new identity, Girls Girls, Chance Chance, Music Music shows how familiar material, treated with sophistication and real perception, sparkles like new.
Eisa Davis’s play and its musician-actor cast explore the compelling variations in four frazzled teenagers’ relationships to music.
The play is fine as far as it goes but it feels like some of the storyline and character development is missing.
Like an important piece of contemporary music, ||: Girls :||: Chance :||: Music :|| is a worthy experiment, even if it’s not the most thrilling thing to sit through.
But as presented, ||: Girls :||: Chance :||: Music :|| feels less of a fully realized play and more like a character study depicting cliquish teen girl behavior and it drags in spots.
As coming-of-age tale or tribute to the importance of art in one’s life, || : Girls : || || : Chance : || || : Music : || impresses.

The audacity of Davis's vision for the play is astounding, beginning with an early scene where the four cast members sing a 12-note tone row whose sequence is determined by audience members placing numbered stickers on a whiteboard of piano keys ahead of the performance.
Still, this is a very special evening of story, song and humanity.
This production makes it hard to come by.
Audiences may have a better night throwing on a favorite jazz record and flipping through old photos than sitting in on this jam session.

cn.t: Davis's intimate portrait of young musicians at a summer program captivates with mesmerizing musicality and raw emotion, though critics split on whether its meandering structure enhances or undermines its exploration of adolescent struggles.

vr.q: It's trying to do too many things all at once. It's spread too thin.
